definition: The Hobbs Act, codified at 18 U.S.C. § 1951, is a key piece of federal criminal legislation regarding the interference with interstate commerce through robbery or extortion. The statute provides for a sentence of not more than 20 years in prison. The Hobbs Act replaced the Copeland Anti-Racketeering Act of 1934, which contained a provision excluding “the payment of wages by a bona-fide employer to a bona-fide employee” from punishment. See United States v. Enmons, 410 U.S. 396 (1973). The U.S. Supreme Court’s interpretation of this provision in United States v. Local 807, 315 U.S. 521 (1942), contributed to subsequent efforts to amend the federal anti-racketeering laws and ultimately led to the enactment of the Hobbs Act. To secure a conviction under the Hobbs Act, the government must generally establish two elements:  The defendant committed or attempted or conspired to commit robbery or extortion, or committed or threatened physical violence against a person or property in furtherance of a robbery or extortion; and  The conduct affected, or in some manner obstructed, delayed, or impacted, interstate or foreign commerce. Under the Hobbs Act, a robbery is the unlawful taking or acquisition of personal property from a person, or in the presence of another, against their will, and by means of actual or threatened force or violence, or fear of injury (immediate or future) to their person or property, or property in their custody or possession, or the person or property of a relative or member of their family, or of anyone in their company at the time of the taking or acquisition. See: 18 U.S.C. § 1951(b)(1). Extortion is the acquisition of property from another, with their consent, but induced through the wrongful use of actual or threatened force, coercion, violence, or fear, or under the color of an official right. See: 18 U.S.C. § 1951(b)(2). The interstate commerce element of the Hobbs Act may vary depending on the nature of the victim and the particular conduct at issue. In Taylor v.
